OneLake Preview versions of Domains REST APIs are no longer available We previously announced March 31, 2026, as the retirement date for the preview versions of Domains REST APIs. As a next step, we changed the default API behavior in August 2026. Requests that don't include the preview query parameter now use the Generally Available (GA) version instead of the preview version. As of November 2026, the preview APIs have been removed completely. Any call that still explicitly requests the preview version will now fail. If your scripts, applications, or automation still use the preview APIs, update them to the GA API contract. Keep in mind that the GA contract includes breaking changes compared to the preview version. This applies to the following APIs: Create Domain, Get Domain, List Domains, and Update Domain. Learn more about these APIs in the Domains REST API documentation . Data Engineering Access data with Power Query in Fabric notebooks (Preview) Fabric notebooks now support running Power Query M queries through existing Fabric connections. Using the new notebookutils.powerquery capability, you can execute an M query and load the results directly into your notebook for further analysis. Gateway-backed connections also enable notebooks to access supported on-premises data sources that are not directly accessible from Fabric compute. The initial release supports read operations from supported data sources. Figur e: Power Query methods available through NotebookUtils in a Fabric notebook. To learn more, refer to the Use Power Query with NotebookUtils in Fabric notebooks documentation. Retrieve Fabric environment publishing logs through the public API (Preview) The Fabric environment public API now supports retrieving publishing logs. You can use the API to access publishing results programmatically, monitor environment publishing in automated workflows, and investigate issues without relying solely on the Fabric user interface. This capability helps teams integrate publishing-log retrieval into automated environment management and lifecycle processes. To learn more, refer to the Retrieve publishing logs using the Fabric environment REST API documentation. Use JFrog Artifactory with Fabric environment items (Preview) Fabric environment items now support JFrog Artifactory as a package repository. Organizations can connect their existing JFrog repositories and use enterprise-managed packages when configuring libraries and dependencies for an environment. This integration helps teams use their established package-management practices in Fabric while providing greater flexibility in how environment dependencies are sourced and managed. Figure : Configuring a JFrog Artifactory connection for use with Fabric environment items. To learn more, refer to the Manage Fabric environment libraries with JFrog Artifactory documentation. Optimal refresh for deletes and updates in Materialized Lake Views (Preview) Materialized Lake Views now extend optimal refresh beyond append-only data. With refresh hints, eligible views can process source deletes and updates incrementally, without recomputing the entire result. For pipelines that remove expired records, update product details, or correct transactions, a small source change no longer must trigger a full recomputation solely because it includes deletes

title: Fabric Data Warehouse at Ignite: Built for AI-era analytics
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Our telemetry shows that agentic analytics has arrived. Agents query, investigate, iterate, test, and drill down without waiting for human input. This machine-paced activity pushes analytical engines built for human-paced workloads to their limits. Fabric Data Warehouse was built from scratch in the 2020s to support this new interaction model, combining highly scalable serverless compute, a resilient lakehouse architecture, and integration across Fabric. At Ignite, we’re building on that foundation for agents and the people who rely on them. The updates focus on performance at agentic scale, better interoperability with AI, and richer capabilities for warehouse development and operations. Scale performance for agentic investigation When queries wait, agentic investigations pause. We’re improving Fabric Data Warehouse performance on three fronts: Fresh OneLake metadata. A faster, more efficient engine. Workload controls that help you balance performance and cost. Keep SQL analytics endpoint metadata fresh The new metadata sync for the SQL analytics endpoint is now generally available. Tables in OneLake are always visible to the SQL analytics endpoint, and queries return fresh data. This release includes: A straightforward upgrade path from existing SQL analytics endpoints. Metadata refreshes within seconds and at query time, so queries always see the latest data. Large object type(LOB) and time travel support. Compatibility with Delta checkpoint V2. Figure: Animated GIF - demonstrating performance of the new SQL analytics endpoint metadata sync. A faster, more efficient engine In recent days we’ve rolled out a rebuilt distributed shuffle to accelerate data movement between query nodes, along with enhanced task scheduling to improve resource use and speed up query tasks. Combined with several earlier innovations, such as distributed bitmap filters and usage-based resource estimation corrections, these changes have improved Fabric Data Warehouse performance by 70% on an industry-standard benchmark[footnoteRef:1] over the past year. Figure: Fabric Data Warehouse performance improvements over time . Controls tailored to your workloads User workloads have varying demands. Some need cached data to stay warm between bursts; others need predictable resource boundaries or acceleration for latency-sensitive analytics. These controls help you make those trade-offs: Cache cooldown (coming in November ) lets you control how long data stays cached at the SQL pool level. Keep data warm between intermittent activity or shorten retention to reduce idle allocation and cost. On-demand billing (Preview) offers consumption-based billing with capacity-level budget controls and workspace-level ceilings. Data Warehouse consumption is separate from other workload categories. When a workspace reaches its ceiling, queries queue and resume as resources become available. Custom SQL pools (Generally Avaiable) , let you set maximum resource shares and separate workloads by application or statement type. Tune SELECT and non-SELECT allocations to match your read/write needs. GPU-based query acceleration ( L imited P review) targets high-concurrency analytical workloads where latency matters, including interactive reporting and AI-driven exploration. Released in August, it delivers roughly twice the performance at one-third lower cost than competing offerings on a 300GB DirectQuery benchmark. Connect Fabric Data Warehouse to the agents you use Develop, query, and operate through AI tools A faster warehouse is even more useful when AI agents can work with it directly. The remote Data Warehouse MCP server gives agents secure high-quality access to your data warehouses . Agent Skills for Microsoft Fabric provide specialized guidance for developing, querying, and operating Fabric items. Together, MCP and Agent Skills bring agent-driven warehouse development, analytics, and operations into the AI tools developers already use. With warehouse-specific capabilities and expertise, agents can carry out end-to-end tasks: explore schemas, write SQL, troubleshoot queries, and manage warehouse workloads. Figure: B ring your own AI tool to Fabric Data Warehouse . Ground answers in shared business context Fabric IQ integration uses ontologies to connect warehouse data with shared business models, concepts, and relationships. This enables Fabric data agents to provide natural-language answers grounded in governed enterprise data. Publish the agents to Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, or custom endpoints to bring insights into the tools where people work and make decisions. Build, operate, and modernize your warehouse with confidence Modern workloads need more than speed and agent access. They also need expressive SQL, clear operational visibility, and dependable tooling for development, governance, and migration. Monitor workloads and troubleshoot queries Workspace monitoring integration, brings warehouses into a shared view and connects workspace-level signals with individual queries. Graphical query plan (coming soon) and Live Query Troubleshooting (Limited Preview) show plans before execution and activity during execution, helping you identify expensive operators and data movement. SQL pool insights enhancements provide near-real-time vNode usage metrics, making compute usage and pool pressure easier to understand. DW monitor enhancements (coming soon) add diagnostic cards that highlight key workload signals and point you to the next troubleshooting step. Operations agent skills help investigate capacity spikes, recommend SQL pools, assess table health, and analyze failures. Write more expressive SQL and simplify development T-SQL enhancements reduce repetition and simplify window-function filtering with FROM-first queries, GROUP BY ALL, and QUALIFY. Regular expressions and analytical aggregates support pattern matching, replacement, and extraction through REGEXP_LIKE, REGEXP_REPLACE, and REGEXP_SUBSTR. For exact and approximate distribution analysis , use MEDIAN, QUANTILE, APPROX_MEDIAN, and APPROX_QUANTILE. User-defined Functions support richer procedural logic with branches, loops, BREAK, and CONTINUE. Eligible functions are inlined, with creation-time checks, actionable errors, control-flow resource estimation, and plan visibility. Fabric User Data Functions integration lets T-SQL call published Python functions to work with APIs, files, configuration, and other Fabric data. Richer data and table support adds VARCHAR(MAX) and VARBINARY(MAX) to the SQL analytics endpoint, supporting text, JSON, logs, and binary content. The SQL web experience introduces table overviews, a no-code table designer, and interactive result visualizations. Redesigned Object Explorer and results grids and improved IntelliSense round out the experience. Figure: Summary of SQL enhancement announcements . Develop, deploy, and govern with greater control Warehouse Clones ( L imited P rivate P review) create point-in-time, read/write environments within or across workspaces and capacities, without an initial full copy. Use them to separate development, testing, reporting, and recovery. Refresh a clone to a newer restore point while retaining its item and endpoint. Sign up to join the Limited Private Preview. Figure: Animated GIF - D emonstrati on of c ross-workspace warehouse cloning in Microsoft Fabric . CI/CD 2.0 with DacFx provides schema-aware deployment and item-definition lifecycle automation for Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint workflows. Use pre- and post-deployment scripts for preparation and validation, and Schema Compare in VS Code to review object differences before deployment. Connectivity and security improvements cover client connections, permissions, identity, and auditing: A more direct client-to-compute

title: Power BI at Ignite: Building on the momentum
text: If you haven't already, read Bogdan Crivat's Microsoft Fabric Ignite blog post for a complete look at our Ignite announcements across Microsoft Fabric. Coming out of FabCon/SQLCon in Barcelona and the Power Platform Community Conference, I'm more excited than ever about what's ahead for Power BI. It's been inspiring to see the community explore new AI-powered experiences and rethink how we interact with data, uncover insights, and make decisions. At FabCon, I shared that Power BI is entering its next chapter. Your ideas, enthusiasm, and feedback since then have helped shape what we're delivering this week. At Ignite, two key parts of that chapter are ready for you to try: Power BI Desktop for Apps and semantic views, both now in public preview. Power BI Desktop for Apps: Build apps where you already build reports In Barcelona, we gave you an early look at a new app-building experience in Power BI Desktop, powered by Fabric apps. This week, it arrives in preview as Power BI Desktop for Apps. It starts where Power BI always has with a semantic model you already trust. Choose a published semantic model, describe the app you want in natural language, and an agent builds it and iterates with you. Refine the result with direct edits and a design pane, preview it locally, and publish it to Microsoft Fabric when it's ready. Because these are apps, they can do more than display data. They can accept inputs, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows. That makes room for everything from a focused portal for a team's reports to a planning app where people enter targets, approve them, and comment in context, all built on the definitions your organization already trusts. Reports aren't going anywhere; they remain the fastest way to explore and share insights. Apps extend what you can build on the same semantic model when people need to act on what they see. This experience isn't limited to Fabric capacity customers. Apps in Power BI are available to Power BI Pro customers in the coming weeks, with support for Premium Per User coming in the months ahead. Fabric apps , the technology underneath, is also now generally available. Figure: Creating an app with the new experience in Power BI Desktop . The apps you build with Power BI Desktop for apps come with a new set of visuals made for Fabric apps. Charts, maps, KPI cards, slicers and data grids share consistent typography, color and spacing, so an app looks cohesive without requiring you to hand-tune every visual. They work in light and dark themes and adapt to your app's own colors. They also behave the way Power BI users expect. With the Fabric visuals packages you get familiar Power BI capabilities like tooltips, cross-filtering and cross-highlighting, so selecting a point in one visual focuses the rest of the page. They support keyboard navigation and screen readers too. To learn more about how we're designing visuals for people and agents alike, refer to the blogpost on Data visualization in the agentic era . Figure: Examples of Fabric visual s capabilities . Semantic views: an open semantic layer, built on Apache Ossie The semantic layer is an organization's most strategic asset. With more than 22 million Power BI semantic models in use every day, Power BI is the world's most widely adopted semantic layer, and the business meaning in those models increasingly grounds agents, apps, and Microsoft Copilot. Today, semantic views enter public preview as the first semantic layer based on Apache Ossie (incubating) open standards, with the unparalleled modeling power of Power BI behind it. You define governed business metrics and semantics directly where your data lives in OneLake, in an open format designed for interoperability. Measures can be written in DAX, so a definition like Total Sales can carry year-over-year and rolling-period logic, not just a simple sum. Define a metric once and reuse it across reports, apps, and AI, within Fabric and, through Apache Ossie, with platforms such as Snowflake and other partners over time. Semantic models remain the heart of Power BI and Fabric IQ. Semantic views complement them by separating business definitions from compute, so the definitions your teams agree on can move across engines and ecosystems without being rebuilt. We'll keep advancing Apache Ossie with Snowflake and the broader community, including establishing DAX as an Ossie-recognized query language. Figure: Defining governed business metrics in a semantic view . What's ahead If you're ready to take the next step and want to learn how to build apps for your teams and organization, we invite you to join Data Days: AI Work​ to learn from practitioners through real projects, working demos, and follow-along sessions. Whether you want to understand the possibilities, find a pattern to try, or share what you build, explore the sessions and find your next step at aka.ms/DataDays . Register for our upcoming Fabric and SQL Community Conferences: Atlanta | Sydney —use code MSCUST to save. Thank you for building with us and for continuing to challenge us to imagine what comes next. I can't wait to see what you create.

title: Run proactive operations with Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. AI is changing how every organization works. For most teams, the hard question isn't whether to use AI. It's how to turn it into real changes in daily operations: fewer surprises, faster responses, and better experiences for customers. Events often arrive faster than any person can respond. In the past, teams were limited by how quickly someone could read an alert and make a call. Now, agents can watch every signal and act in seconds, and each action and its outcome feed back into the system so it improves over time. This isn't only about factory floors or connected devices. Every organization has events it wants to respond to: Catch an issue before it happens, such as a shipment running late or a system nearing capacity. Monitor processes and systems for anomalies, enabling a fix before something breaks. Automate entire workflows instead of handing work between teams. Improve the customer experience while the customer is still engaged. TransGrid Energy uses Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence to turn live data-center telemetry into better operational outcomes. By bringing power, cooling, battery, and equipment data together with real-time alarm rules and its WattSchema ontology, TransGrid can identify potential failures before they happen and optimize cooling or battery use as operating conditions and energy prices change. Data-center operators can improve uptime, efficiency, and cost control without building and maintaining complex data-movement infrastructure. “We want to focus on our business problems, not our data movement problems. Fabric Real-Time Intelligence handles this for us so we can focus on our business” Tony Guidici - CTO / Head of Digital Service, TransGrid Energy, LLC At Ignite, we're announcing new capabilities in Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric that make it simpler to stream, analyze, and act on event data. We're helping our customers move from waiting for something to fail and reacting, to predicting that it might fail and getting ahead of it. Figure: Real-Time Intelligence connects streaming, analysis, and action in a continuous loop. Stream: Connect to real-time data wherever it lives Every organization already has streaming data, from applications, databases, devices, and logs. For years, putting it to work was a project of its own. The data lived across clouds and systems, and every source needed its own pipeline. Ingesting, storing, querying, and alerting each took a separate tool, with its own security model, its own bill, and its own specialists. The cost and complexity stalled many projects before they delivered anything. Real-Time Intelligence changes that. Working with streaming data no longer takes a specialist. With Eventstream , you can connect Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, MQTT, and database change data capture, then filter, transform, and route events without writing code. If it produces events, Fabric can take them. Real-Time hub , built into every Fabric tenant, gives you one place to discover and manage all of it, with nothing to set up. And because it's part of Fabric, streaming data gets the same security, governance, and cost management as the rest of your data. What's new for s treaming Event Hubs shortcuts (Preview) Many teams already run their event pipelines on Azure Event Hubs. We're introducing Event Hubs shortcuts so you can bring an event hub you already run into Fabric as an eventstream, without an extra copy. You keep control in Azure, and you can filter, transform, and route events to Eventhouse, lakehouse, Activator, and more. Native Eventstream routing endpoint in Azure IoT Hub (Generally Available) Many device solutions already send their telemetry through Azure IoT Hub. Eventstream is now a native routing endpoint in IoT Hub, so you can send device data straight into Fabric using the routing rules, filters, and message enrichments you already have. You get from device telemetry to real-time insights, alerts, and automated actions faster, and you can combine telemetry with device-state events for a fuller view of your operations. Figure: Fabric Eventstream is now a native endpoint in Azure IoT Hub for message routing. Business events as a source and destination in Eventstream (Generally Available) Some of the most useful signals are business moments, like a shipment running late. Business events let you define them once and share them across Fabric. We're making them generally available as both a source and a destination in Eventstream, so you can route business events like any other stream, or turn live data into new ones that Activator, notebooks, and other Fabric items act on. Together, these updates let you use the streams you already have and turn them into signals the rest of Fabric can act on. Figure: Bringing an existing Azure event hub into Fabric as an eventstream . Analyze: Make sense of fast-changing data Analyzing real-time data is different from analyzing a nightly report. Events arrive in high volume, often as semi-structured JSON or logs, and the questions change as conditions change. Tools built for batch reporting weren't designed for that. By the time the data was loaded and modeled, the moment had passed, and stale data isn't insight. It's history. Operational data is complex. Understanding it shouldn't be. Eventhouse is purpose-built for event, log, and time-series data, with sub-second queries at petabyte scale, so you can ask new questions of fresh data in KQL or SQL, or in plain language with Copilot. Real-Time Dashboards show what's happening as it happens, and Fabric Maps show where. And because it all sits on OneLake, your real-time data isn't siloed from the rest of your data estate. Figure: A Real-Time Dashboard and map showing what's happening, and where, as it happens. What's new for a nalysis Outbound access protection and Customer-Managed Keys for Eventhouse (Generally Available) Real-time workloads need the same protections as the rest of your data. We're extending two of them to every Eventhouse scenario. Customer-Managed Keys (CMK) give you direct control over the encryption keys that protect your data and metadata in Eventhouse. Outbound access protection blocks Eventhouse from sending data anywhere you haven't explicitly allowed, now including connections to Event Hubs and Eventstream, which helps prevent data exfiltration. Smart caching and update policies for OneLake shortcuts in Eventhouse (Preview) Eventhouse can query data where it already lives in OneLake through shortcuts , and query acceleration keeps those queries fast. We're making that smarter and simpler. Eventhouse now tunes the acceleration cache automatically based on real query patterns, instead of a fixed, manually set window, so frequently queried data stays fast and you get better price-performance with no tuning. And you can now attach update policies to accelerated shortcuts, so transformations run continuously as new data lands in the lake, with no separate pipeline. Together, these updates let you analyze real-time data with the same protections as the rest of your estate and get fast answers from the data you already have in OneLake. Proactive Eventhouse monitoring (Preview) To optimize your real-time setup, you need a clear, at-a-glance view of what's happening, so you can react appropriately. Three new Workspace Monitoring logs give you that visibility: Capacity Throttling Events – Identify when an Eventhouse enters throttling and understand the different throttling stages. Sub-Optimal Eventhouse Size – Detect when an Eventhouse remains undersized due to capacity constraints, signaling a need for capacity or workload optimization. title: Build and operate intelligent apps with Microsoft Fabric: New capabilities at Ignite 2026
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. AI-powered development tools are making it faster than ever to build applications. But moving from prototype to production remains challenging. Developers still need to connect applications to enterprise data, secure access, manage databases, and ensure applications can operate reliably at scale. At Microsoft Ignite, we're introducing new capabilities in Microsoft Fabric that bring application development, operational databases, and database management closer together, helping teams build and operate intelligent applications with less complexity. We are announcing three important milestones toward that vision: Fabric apps (Generally Available) , helps developers and coding agents build and deploy complete business applications with enterprise data, security, and governance built in, using the open-source Rayfin SDK and CLI. Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB (Preview) , brings serverless PostgreSQL to Fabric for the dynamic workloads of modern applications and AI agents. Database Hub in Fabric (Generally Available) , provides a unified experience to discover, monitor, and manage databases, with database agents for SQL and PostgreSQL now in preview. Together, these innovations simplify the journey from idea to production and bring greater intelligence to database operations. Move from prompt to production with Fabric apps Fabric apps (Generally Available) , give developers and coding agents a simpler path to building and deploying complete business applications. Developers and coding agents can build Fabric apps with Rayfin, the open-source SDK and CLI that provides backend capabilities including databases, authentication, functions, storage, and observability. When deployed to Fabric, these applications become Fabric apps, connecting application experiences with enterprise data and governance in Microsoft Fabric. Since launching in preview just five months ago, more than 100,000 Fabric apps have been created . Figure: Animated GIF - Examples of data-rich business applications built with Microsoft Fabric apps. Build on trusted enterprise data Fabric apps connect to existing semantic models, warehouses, and lakehouses, allowing developers to build on trusted business data without recreating data models or access controls. Teams can extend analytics into interactive applications that support business workflows, enabling users to move from understanding what's happening to taking action. With general availability, we're also introducing enhanced security and governance capabilities. A new Apps view in the OneLake Governance hub gives administrators visibility into applications across their organization, with the ability to block or unblock them. Content Security Policy settings and private sites provide additional protection. We're also making it easier to build Fabric-powered applications from the tools people already use. With Microsoft Copilot, builders can go from a simple prompt to a working application, with the option to use Fabric as a ready-to-use data backend for databases, storage, and data APIs. Integrations with Power BI Desktop will also help teams turn trusted semantic models into interactive business applications. Customers are already seeing the potential. “Rayfin aligns closely with Hitachi Energy’s long-term vision for a unified data, analytics, and AI platform built on Microsoft Fabric. Rayfin provides a compelling way to move beyond traditional reporting and deliver Fabric-native operational experiences that bring together data, insights, and business processes.” —Niek Brasa, Chief Architect at Hitachi Energy Learn more about the new capabilities and how to get started in the Rayfin and Fabric apps blog post . Serverless PostgreSQL in Fabric, built for intelligent applications Developers have always built applications on databases, but agents are now building them at an entirely different speed. Agents spin up databases for prototypes, experiments, and short-lived tasks, then drop them when the work is done. Most of these workloads start small, run in bursts, and sit idle between uses, which makes their compute needs hard to predict and inefficient to run continually. Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB is serverless and built for exactly these scenarios, with: Rapid provisioning: Databases provision in seconds so developers and agents can start building immediately. Automatic pause: Compute pauses after five minutes of inactivity to avoid keeping resources running between tasks. On-demand resume: Compute resumes when the next query arrives without manual intervention. Fabric HorizonDB is also available as a PostgreSQL database for Fabric apps. Its serverless architecture gives developers and coding agents a database that can be provisioned quickly, scales with application demand, and pauses when not in use, without requiring them to manage the underlying infrastructure. Once those applications are running, they need more than their own operational data. Fabric HorizonDB now supports translytical capabilities on OneLake to operationalize lake data, bringing the scale and performance of Fabric's analytical engines to live transactions through: Translytical queries: PostgreSQL queries are transparently converted to run on Fabric Data Warehouse, using distributed, scale-out execution on CPU- or GPU-powered processing. Analytical queries can run an order of magnitude faster or more than they would natively in PostgreSQL. Full and partial pushdown are both supported, so a single query can join PostgreSQL tables with data in OneLake. Mirroring: Fabric HorizonDB tables are replicated into OneLake by default and are automatically converted to Delta format, so data is ready for translytical application workloads and large-scale analytics across Fabric without building data integration pipelines. Synced Tables: Enriched data from Fabric Data Warehouse flows back into HorizonDB (reverse ETL) for low-latency, high-concurrency serving to applications and agents. Snapshot sync handles periodic refreshes such as daily scores or aggregates, while the continuous sync option keeps tables current as source data changes. Figure: Fabric HorizonDB unifies operational and analytical data through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, enabling applications to query, analyze, and act on data across Fabric and OneLake. Together, serverless compute and translytical capabilities on OneLake give applications and agents a single PostgreSQL endpoint for working across live operational data and analytical data in Fabric. They can start small, scale with demand, and act on transactions and insights without building separate data pipelines or managing database infrastructure. Opsen AI, for example, is exploring how these capabilities can help financial services firms respond faster to payment and trade exceptions. “As settlement cycles shorten and financial services become more automated, resolving payment and trade exceptions requires more than the current transaction state. Fabric HorizonDB enables us to connect operational data with historical insights in OneLake to provide firms with the broader business context to resolve exceptions faster and make more informed decisions.” — Jennings Balavari, Founder and CEO, Opsen AI Learn more in this Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB blog post . Database professionals need a simpler way to manage growing database estates, monitor performance, and troubleshoot issues without switching between multiple tools. title: Microsoft Fabric is Fueling Frontier Transformation
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. I am elated to be stepping into an expanded role leading Microsoft Fabric at an important moment for our customers and our data community. Organizations everywhere are moving beyond experimenting with AI and beginning to reimagine how people, applications, and agents work together. What is becoming increasingly clear to everyone is that this transformation starts with data: trusted, governed, and connected to the context of how each business operates. Customers are moving quickly in this direction. More than 44,000 paid customers now use Microsoft Fabric, an increase of more than 50 percent year over year. More than 19,000 customers are also using Microsoft Foundry and Fabric together, connecting intelligent applications and agents to the operational, analytical, and unstructured data that powers their businesses. That momentum is exciting, but it also reinforces our responsibility to make the data foundation simpler, more open, and more useful for everyone who builds and works with it. Today at Microsoft Ignite, we are introducing the next wave of innovation across Microsoft Fabric. These announcements bring together the broader Microsoft data story: unifying operational and analytical data, giving that data shared business context, and helping organizations turn trusted insights into action. Together, they show how Fabric is evolving to fuel Frontier Transformation through its deepening connection to Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft IQ, giving IT leaders the control they need and practitioners the tools to build what comes next. Help every agent understand how your business works with Fabric IQ Every organization has access to the same frontier models. What sets yours apart is the knowledge only your business has: how your processes run, how you define your metrics and how you serve your customers. That knowledge lives across documents and procedures, conversations in Microsoft 365, systems of record and the data your analysts model. Because it's scattered, every new agent starts from zero and teams keep rebuilding the same groundwork. Today at Microsoft Ignite, we're introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform that helps you turn that knowledge into your own IQ. It captures and governs what your business knows, so every AI app and agent you build can reuse it. With new business plugins, available through the Frontier program, teams can bundle what they know into trusted, reusable context, skills and tools and share them across the business. Domain experts write a business plugin once, and every agent can use it. Fabric IQ brings the meaning of your business data to Microsoft IQ. It models the entities, relationships, metrics and rules that define your business, building on the Power BI semantic models and Fabric data you run today. Agents work from the same definitions your analysts use, so answers stay consistent from one agent to the next. We’re introducing semantic views, now in preview, as the first semantic layer based on Apache Ossie open standards. With our deep heritage in semantic modeling with Power BI, we are making the unparalleled modeling power of Power BI broadly available to the data estate through this announcement. You define governed business metrics and semantics directly where your data lives in OneLake, in an open format designed for interoperability. We're also bringing Fabric IQ to more of the places your teams work. Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Copilot are already generally available, and Fabric data agents are coming to Copilot, with general availability coming soon. Copilot Chat and Cowork users get Fabric IQ without consuming additional Copilot Credits. In Microsoft Excel, you can turn on Fabric IQ in Edit with Copilot, in preview, to query governed semantic models and build live, Fabric-connected PivotTables. New Fabric IQ connectors, also in preview, bring the same insights into ChatGPT and Claude. Figure: Animated GIF - In Microsoft Copilot Chat, a user attaches a Fabric data agent to a prompt and gets an answer grounded in the organization's business data, combined with context from Work IQ. "We are strongly impressed by the very detailed and actionable insights Microsoft Copilot Chat is providing on top of our Power BI semantic models. Excited to really start harvesting our Power BI footprint investments now!" — Stijn Lioen, Global Architect Data & Analytics, Mohawk Industries For developers, Fabric Apps is now (Generally Available), and you can embed conversational experiences powered by semantic models and Fabric data agents into your apps, in (Preview) Ontologies in Fabric IQ are now in GitHub Copilot, in preview, so the code it writes reflects how your business works. Fabric IQ MCP, now (Generally Available), connects any compatible agent or app to Fabric IQ under your existing Fabric permissions. Fabric IQ MCP and Skills for Fabric now also support data agents and ontologies, in (Preview). IQ sharing in Fabric (Preview), now let’s organizations share ontologies with other enterprises, so business context can move across company boundaries along with the data. Partners can build an ontology once and share it with their customers, who can use that business context right away without recreating the underlying definitions. Financial Fabric, TomTom, xMentium, EY, and Sitecore are building IQ sharing in Fabric integrations, with availability coming soon. Go deeper on Microsoft IQ: Read the Microsoft IQ launch blog post to learn how it helps organizations build, run, and continuously improve AI apps and agents . The next opportunity is helping people and agents use that context to create applications that solve real business problems. Today, Rayfin and Fabric apps are (Generally Available), making it easier for developers and agents to turn enterprise data into production-ready applications. Since launching in preview, builders have already created more than 100,000 apps, demonstrating the growing demand for faster, simpler ways to build applications grounded in business data. Rayfin provides the open-source SDK and CLI for developers and AI agents to build and deploy applications to Microsoft Fabric. Fabric apps provide the managed application experience, with built-in backend services, enterprise data connectivity, security, and governance. At Ignite, we are expanding these capabilities into the tools where people already work, making application development accessible to more developers, business users, and agents. With the new Microsoft Copilot integration, rolling out in Frontier preview, business users can build apps directly in Copilot, with the option to use Fabric as the backend providing databases, storage, and data APIs. This creates a direct path from an idea developed through Copilot to a working application, without requiring users to assemble the underlying infrastructure. Apps built in Microsoft Copilot that require these advanced capabilities will consume Copilot Credits for the underlying Fabric services . title: Build governed data apps with Microsoft Fabric Apps (Generally Available)
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. AI has made it much faster to create an initial version of an app. Ask a coding agent to turn the spreadsheet your team uses to track supplier issues into an app, and it can be running in hours rather than days. Putting that app in front of the business is another matter. It needs a database, sign-in, and access to company data that respects the permissions already in place, and IT needs to know the app exists. Left to wire this up alone, an agent takes the shortest path, which often means copying data where it shouldn’t go or sharing it with people who shouldn’t see it. Multiply that by every team with an agent and you get shadow IT at agent speed. Rayfin and Microsoft Fabric apps address these deployment and governance challenges, and today at Microsoft Ignite, both are generally available. Developers and their agents build with Rayfin, our open-source SDK and CLI. When deployed, the app runs as a Fabric app, next to your data, behind Microsoft Entra sign-in, and under the governance you already have. We want every team to build like a startup and deploy like an enterprise. Since preview, more than 100,000 apps have been created. Today’s release makes Rayfin and Fabric apps ready for production and adds PostgreSQL and file storage for developers, a single view of every app for administrators, and new ways to build from Microsoft Copilot and Power BI. Figure: Animated GIF - Examples of data-rich business applications built with Microsoft Fabric apps. More examples can be found in the Fabric apps community gallery . The whole app, defined in code With Rayfin, the backend lives in the same project as the user interface. You describe your data and who can access it in TypeScript, and Rayfin generates the database and API with those rules enforced. One command, Rayfin up, deploys the whole app to Fabric. We built it this way on purpose. It gives coding agents a consistent development model instead of requiring them to coordinate multiple cloud services independently. And because every app declares its data, permissions, and connections in one place, it’s easier to review and govern. Figure: Rayfin defines app data, APIs, authentication, policies, functions, and hosting for local or Fabric deployment. Every Fabric app can use: Databases: SQL database in Fabric, or the new Fabric HorizonDB (Preview), serverless PostgreSQL for teams and agents that default to Postgres. Authentication and permissions : Microsoft Entra sign-in and per-record access rules. Functions : server-side TypeScript for business logic, integrations, and calls to Microsoft Foundry models. Connectors : direct access to the semantic models, warehouses, lakehouses, and SQL databases you already have in Fabric. Storage : files, images, and documents, stored in OneLake. Observability: metrics, logs, and traces in Application Insights. Because the app is defined in code, developers can use the same project across local and cloud environments. Rayfin Local runs the app and its back end on your laptop, even before you have a Fabric workspace. The Rayfin up command then publishes the same code to Fabric unchanged. The model is similar to developing in Power BI Desktop and publishing to the Power BI service: creators work locally and deploy to a managed service when they are ready to share. That shared development model is already helping organizations reduce the handoffs between data experts and engineers. The Craneware Group , which helps healthcare providers optimize their financial performance, previously lost days or weeks as ideas moved between customers, data experts, engineering, and production. With Fabric apps, its data experts can build alongside engineers on a shared, governed foundation, helping ideas move from review to deployment without the wait. “Fabric apps are changing the way we think about application development. Instead of treating data, analytics, AI, and the application as separate technology stacks, we can bring them together on a single governed platform and focus our engineering effort on creating value for customers.” —Mark Sentell, VP of Product Development, The Craneware Group Built on the data you already trust Most organizations have spent years getting their data right, from certified semantic models to agreed definitions of revenue and margin. Fabric apps build on that work instead of starting over with another copy. A Fabric app can query the same semantic models and measures as your Power BI reports, while retaining the security defined for that data. With the new Fabric IQ connector, people can also ask about that data in plain language. And decisions made in the app can be written back to governed tables in OneLake, ready for reporting and AI. That foundation is already changing how teams put trusted data into action. At Thomson Reuters , the Monthly Business Review now runs as a Fabric app, built on the same certified Power BI semantic models that ground the company’s DeepVista AI framework and its agents in Microsoft Teams. By bringing trusted metrics, natural-language analysis, and review workflows into a single experience, the team spends less time reconciling numbers and more time deciding what to do next. “This is a breakthrough in how Finance works. Certified semantic models give us numbers we can trust. Thomson Reuters DeepVista’s AI agents let analysts and leaders ask questions in natural language and get insights they can act on. The monthly business hub solution automates the business review, so we spend our time on what to do next.” —Michael Goddard, Head of Corporate Finance, Thomson Reuters Watch the interview with Thomson Reuters to see how they are innovating with Fabric. Governed by default As more people build with AI, apps will multiply faster than any IT team can review them one at a time. The controls have to live in the platform, not in a review queue. Every Fabric app is a Fabric item, so it shows up in lineage, follows your workspace permissions and sharing rules, and runs on your capacity. Capabilities for administrators with general availability: The Apps view in the OneLake governance hub: every app in the organization in one place, with the ability to block or unblock any of them. Content Security Policy (CSP): control over which external resources an app can load in the browser. Secure Embed: the option to require that apps run only inside an embedded frame. Item identity: apps reach data under their own identity, not the permissions of the person who deployed them. Figure: Manage and govern Fabric apps across your organization with the Apps view in the OneLake Governance hub. Build wherever you work Professional developers will build in code with the agent they prefer. But many of the most useful apps will come from the people closest to the work, like the analyst who owns the forecast. They should be able to start in familiar Microsoft experiences and build on the same governed foundation. Microsoft Copilot: Turn a simple prompt into a working application, with the option to use Fabric as a managed backend for databases, storage, and data APIs through Copilot Managed Runtime. Apps can grow from simple ideas into data-rich business solutions without managing infrastructure. Power BI: We’re bringing Fabric apps to Power BI Pro, so many more Power BI users can build them. Power BI Desktop for apps turns an existing semantic model into an interactive app that runs on Fabric. Get started I expect that within a few years, building an app will be as ordinary as building a spreadsheet. When that happens, making an app enterprise-ready can’t be a separate project. title: OneLake: The unified foundation for data, context, governance, and AI
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Most organizations' data is scattered across dozens of applications, clouds and services. Now that agents need to work across the entire business, organizations need to bring that data together in one place: one copy, open to every engine and team, without moving or duplicating it. Unified data gives agents reach, but to act with confidence they also need context: what the data means, how it connects to the business, who should see it and whether it can be trusted. OneLake is the single place for customers to unify their data estate. Shortcuts , mirroring , catalog federation and IQ Share bring multi-cloud, on-premises sources and databases and data platforms together into a single view of the data estate. The OneLake catalog provides a trusted place for organizations to easily explore, govern and secure data in OneLake. It's integrated with every Fabric workload and one of the only lakes that governs data in both Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg open formats, making it truly open. Users can bring popular analytics and AI products and open-source projects to open data in OneLake. Figure: OneLake provides an open, governed foundation for Fabric workloads. OneLake handles over 11 0 b i l l i on int er a c tion s a d ay , and data stored natively in OneLake is backed by 4 million storage accounts. In addition, more than 240,000 organizations use the OneLake catalog to govern more than 350 million data items. The catalog is embedded in more than 100 apps people use every day, including Foundry, Power BI, Teams, and Excel. At Microsoft Ignite, we're taking the next step and making OneLake catalog the center of Microsoft's data governance strategy , delivering new capabilities that bring data, context, and governance together for AI, and expanding the partner ecosystem that extends OneLake across the wider data estate. Here's what that means to you. The OneLake Catalog: Governance where your data lives Customers have told us consistently that running a standalone catalog alongside their data platform creates friction, and that they want governance to live where data is analyzed and put to work. The market has moved the same way, with leading data platforms building governance directly into the analytics experience. Fabric has always had a lake-first data foundation with OneLake, and OneLake catalog already has market leading governance and administration. Figure : OneLake catalog brings data discovery, governance and security together on OneLake, with Copilot built in. This is where Microsoft has strong momentum. We’re making a definitive announcement: OneLake catalog is now Microsoft’s data governance product . This isn't something new either. The OneLake catalog has been the trusted catalog for Fabric data for years, and we're now deepening our investment in it. From a single place, teams can deliver on three main tasks: Explore : Easily discover and understand data across the estate, with lineage, permissions and business context on every item. Govern : See governance insights and recommended actions , and manage domains, tags, endorsements and policies centrally. Secure : Manage OneLake security roles and fine-grained permissions in one central hub . As part of this data governance evolution, Microsoft Purview Data Governance will be retired , and new data governance innovation will land in the OneLake catalog. We want to be clear about what this means. The OneLake catalog takes a different approach: rather than cataloging metadata wherever it lives, it governs the data that lives in or is connected to OneLake through native items, federated catalogs, IQ Shares, Shortcuts and Mirrored databases. That makes it a new model, not a feature-for-feature replacement for Purview Data Governance. Purview Data Security and Compliance, including Information Protection, Data Loss Prevention, Insider Risk Management and Data Security Posture Management, are not affected and continue to protect your data in Fabric. OneLake catalog brings discovery, governance, and security together where data is managed and used. Generally available capabilities help teams find and understand trusted data, monitor governance health, and enforce consistent protections. Govern Skills help identify gaps and prioritize action. We have enhanced further with richer discovery across granular data objects, improved search and lineage, and new Curation and Protection Skills. These skills extend AI-assisted governance beyond health assessments, helping organizations improve metadata quality, identify protection gaps, and take action with AI assistance. Together, these capabilities make it easier to find trusted data, understand how it's being used, and manage governance and security at scale. With Data governance being a core priority for us and our customers – we will continue expanding these capabilities with Data Quality, enhanced curation with glossaries, enhanced granular lineage, additional policies for guardrails, and more. All with the goal to allow governing your data at scale and ensuring your data is ready for AI. Strategic partnership with Atlan to extend data governance Today we are announcing a strategic partnership with Atlan aligned with our lake-first data governance approach. OneLake and Fabric customers can use Atlan, Microsoft’s preferred data governance partner, to extend governance beyond OneLake. The OneLake catalog provides native governance across Fabric and connected data, while Atlan complements it across the broader data estate. Atlan also provides granular, cross-estate lineage and richer governance constructs such as usage and popularity stats across heterogeneous, non-Microsoft data sources, and supports customers transitioning from Purview Data Governance to Fabric with tooling to carry their existing metadata forward. Figure: OneLake and Atlan provide complementary governance across the broader data estate. Governance gives organizations confidence in their data. The next step is making that data, and the context around it, ready for AI. New in OneLake: Bringing data and context together for AI Governance is the foundation, but AI needs more than well-governed tables. Agents need the context and permissions that travel with the data. Today we're introducing new OneLake capabilities that close that gap: IQ sharing in OneLake and Fabric (Preview) At FabCon Barcelona, we introduced IQ sharing, which lets organizations share data and context with other Fabric tenants without copying data. Partners such as S&P Global, TomTom, EY, xMentium, Sitecore, Xoople, and Financial Fabric use it to prepare their data and expertise once and deliver it to many customers in Fabric by listing their integrations in OneLake catalog. Now IQ Sharing adds Fabric IQ O ntologies as an Item that customers can share, so providers can share the business entities, relationships and definitions that describe their data along with the data itself. Figure : Animated GIF - Sharing data with other Fabric tenants through IQ sharing . AI Search (Microsoft Foundry) support for OneLake with OneLake security (Preview) Agents built in Microsoft Foundry can use data stored in OneLake. The OneLake catalog is available in Foundry, and OneLake items, including shortcuts and mirrored items, can be added as knowledge sources in Foundry IQ (Preview) . With OneLake catalog embedded in Microsoft Foundry, developers can explore enterprise data with rich metadata, endorsements, and sensitivity labels, then easily connect trusted data to their AI agents while respecting existing permissions and governance. title: Bringing trusted Fabric IQ context to wherever people and agents work
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Over the past year, AI has moved from answering questions to doing the work. As the 2026 Microsoft Work Trend Index shows, people are now handing entire tasks to agents and directing several at once. Those agents plan, decide, and act across systems, with less human review at every step. Fabric IQ helps turn your organization's business knowledge into an advantage for people and agents. As agents take on more responsibility, that knowledge matters more than which model they run on. Every organization can use the same frontier models. What sets yours apart is its context layer: the definitions, metrics, relationships, and rules that describe how your business actually works. When you connect that context with knowledge from across the organization, people and agents can uncover insights and take informed action that reflects how the business operates. The organizations seeing results treat business context as shared infrastructure, built once and reused by every agent. Today at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we're extending the reach of Fabric IQ, the part of Microsoft IQ that captures how your business operates, to more of the places where that work happens, including Microsoft Copilot, Excel, ChatGPT and Codex by OpenAI, Claude by Anthropic, Fabric apps, and GitHub Copilot. We're also strengthening every foundation beneath it, from Microsoft OneLake and semantic models to ontologies and Fabric agents, so the context your teams define can power every agent that follows. Fabric IQ and Microsoft IQ A common challenge in getting agents into production is that the context, data, models, and runtime they depend on sit in silos, so teams end up rebuilding them for every project. Microsoft IQ , which we're introducing today, is the enterprise context management platform that helps organizations build their own IQ by capturing, governing, and reusing the business knowledge their apps and agents depend on. It connects context from Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ, so every agent starts from what your organization already knows. New business plugins let teams package that knowledge into context, skills, and tools that colleagues across the business can trust and reuse. Learn more in Yitzhak Kesselman and Tina Schuchman’s Microsoft IQ blog post . Within Microsoft IQ, Fabric IQ models how your business operates. It powers a continuous loop where people and agents observe live signals, reason over shared context, and take governed action across analytics, operations, and the tools where work happens. It brings together three layers of business context and the agents that put it to work: Unified data: Microsoft OneLake brings analytical and operational data together in a single, accessible layer. Business intelligence: Power BI semantic models provide the governed metrics and definitions organizations already use to measure their business. Operational intelligence: Ontologies define business entities, their relationships, and the rules that govern them, so agents can reason in the language of the business. With live signals from Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, they also reflect what's happening right now. Agents sit on top of these layers and put that context to work. Specialized agents add expertise of their own: Fabric data agents answer natural-language questions the way the teams who know the data best would, and operations agents monitor live data and recommend action when conditions change. Broader agents like Microsoft Copilot combine Fabric IQ with the rest of Microsoft IQ, such as emails, meetings, and documents, to complete work that spans the business. Bring trusted business context to more experiences with Fabric IQ The business questions people ask don't change based on where they ask them. With Fabric IQ, conversational analytics draws on the same business context wherever people and agents work. New integrations across Microsoft and third-party experiences carry the context your teams define once into more of the tools they use every day, so insights and actions rest on the same understanding of the business. Grounding Microsoft Copilot in your business with data agents (General Availability) Coming Soon Every day, millions of business users turn to Microsoft Copilot to find information, analyze data, and get work done. For many, it has become the first place they go to understand what's happening in the business. As people hand Copilot larger, multistep tasks, an answer that uses the wrong definition of revenue, or misses how a delay ripples through operations, can send a decision in the wrong direction. Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Copilot are already generally available, so answers reflect the metrics your organization has agreed on. Next, we're bringing Fabric data agents to Microsoft Copilot, with general availability coming soon. Anyone in Copilot Chat or Cowork will be able to get specialist answers from agents your teams have configured by simply attaching a data agent. And with Work IQ , Copilot can combine this business context with the emails, meetings, and documents around a decision. Figure: Animated GIF - In Microsoft Copilot Chat, a user attaches a Fabric data agent to a prompt and gets an answer grounded in the organization's business data, combined with context from Work IQ. Bringing Fabric IQ to ChatGPT and Claude (Preview) Coming Soon Many organizations use Microsoft Copilot alongside other AI assistants. That’s why we are introducing Fabric IQ plugins for ChatGPT and Claude , in preview coming soon, which bring insights from Power BI semantic models directly into both assistants. Users can ask questions of their enterprise data without opening a report, and answers draw on the measures your analysts already maintain, so a revenue figure in ChatGPT or Claude matches the one in your quarterly business review. Figure: Animated GIF - In ChatGPT, a user connects the Fabric IQ plugin, asks it to find reports about inventory, and gets back the matching Power BI report. Bringing Fabric IQ to Excel (Insiders Beta) Excel is still where much of the business’s planning and forecasting happens, and with Copilot in Excel, more of those workbooks are now built through conversation. Figures exported from a report go stale quickly, though, and definitions drift each time they're copied. title: The next chapter for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse (Preview)
text: Building and operating a data warehouse is increasingly a software engineering discipline. Teams want to develop warehouse changes in isolation, version them in Git, review them through pull requests, promote them safely across environments, and automate the entire process using their existing CI/CD systems. Over the past several releases, we've been evolving CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse around that lifecycle: DacFx established a common schema deployment foundation. Pre, and post-deployment scripts expanded deployments beyond schema changes. Warehouse Item Definition APIs opened the same lifecycle to automation. Together, these investments are creating a more complete CI/CD lifecycle for Fabric Warehouse, from developing and versioning database changes to deploying and automating them across environments. Let’s take a closer look at how each capability moves that experience forward, what’s available today, and what we’re building next. What we've delivered Establishing a consistent deployment foundation with DacFx The first challenge was making Warehouse deployments behave like database deployments, not artifact copies. A Warehouse contains state, data, dependencies, and relationships between database objects. Moving a change from development to production therefore requires understanding what changed and how those changes should be applied to the target database . This is where DacFx became foundational to the experience. With Git Integration , it is represented as a SQL database project in source control. Developers can work using familiar Git practices such as branching, commits, and pull requests. When those changes are synchronized back to Fabric, DacFx understands the database model and determines the schema changes that need to be applied. Figure: Git-based development workflow in Microsoft Fabric , enabling isolated feature development, collaboration through pull requests, and synchronization of Fabric items across feature and shared workspaces, with infrastructure managed as code. We extended that same foundation to deployment pipelines . When a Warehouse moves between development, test and production environments, DacFx compares source and target states and generates the incremental deployment required to move the target to the desired state. Figure: End-to-end CI/CD workflow in Microsoft Fabric , combining Git-based feature development with deployment pipelines to promote Fabric items consistently across development, test, and production environments. That established a consistent path: Develop → Version in Git → Review → Deploy → Validate → Promote. Pre, and post-deployment scripts A production deployment rarely consists of schema changes alone. Teams often need to prepare data before a deployment, seed or initialize data afterward, or execute SQL actions that need to happen at a specific point in the release. To support that workflow, we introduced pre, and post-deployment scripts . A shared SQL query can be designated as a pre, or post-deployment script and becomes part of the SQL project. The designation travels with the Warehouse through Git, allowing those actions to be versioned and deployed together with the database definition. The resulting deployment lifecycle becomes pre-deployment actions → DacFx schema deployment → post-deployment actions Figure: Pre, and post-deployment script configuration in Fabric Warehouse , enabling developers to define SQL scripts that execute automatically before and after schema deployment as part of the CI/CD lifecycle. This moves more of the database release process into the CI/CD definition rather than leaving teams to coordinate separate manual steps. Learn more about pre and post-deployment scripts . Warehouse Item Definition APIs Git integration and deployment pipelines provide built-in Fabric experiences, but enterprise CI/CD also needs to work outside the Fabric portal. Customers have existing build systems, automation frameworks and release pipelines and need a programmatic way to manage Warehouse definitions. Warehouse Item Definition APIs are the next part of that foundation. Warehouse definitions support SQL project and DACPAC formats , and Fabric APIs can be used to create a Warehouse from a definition, retrieve its current definition, or update it programmatically. Learn more about the Warehouse REST APIs . This means the same Warehouse definition that underpins Git integration can also participate in API-driven CI/CD workflows. Bringing Familiar Warehouse Development Experiences to Client Tools A complete CI/CD experience starts well before deployment. Developers need familiar tools to build, compare, validate, and manage database changes throughout the development lifecycle. Alongside our DacFx investments, we've strengthened Fabric Warehouse support across SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and Visual Studio Code , bringing familiar SQL development workflows closer to the Fabric web experience. These investments include: Database project support in SSMS: Develop and manage Warehouse schemas using SQL database projects and familiar database development workflows. Schema Compare in VS Code: Compare database schemas, review differences, and generate the changes needed to synchronize environments. Consistent database development: Use the same SQL project and DacFx foundation whether developing in the Fabric portal or client tools. Pre, and post-deployment scripts: Maintain deployment scripts as part of the database project, enabling a consistent deployment experience across web-based and client-based development workflows. The goal is simple: developers should be able to choose their preferred development environment without changing how their database projects are versioned, built, or deployed. This brings together the flexibility of familiar SQL development tools with the integrated CI/CD experience in Fabric Warehouse. What's next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse Building on this foundation, we’re focusing on three investments: Deployment configurations: Give developers control over how changes are applied. Cover data handling, object handling, and error handling. Apply different behaviors per environment, such as permissive in development and stricter in production. Fabric CI/CD package (fabric-cicd) support for Warehouse: Simplify end-to-end automation. Deploy Warehouse definitions from source control alongside other Fabric items. Integrate with systems like Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions. CI/CD for SQL analytics endpoint: Extend Git integration and deployment pipelines using the same SQL project and DacFx foundation. Lay the groundwork for coordinated deployments across dependent Fabric items in medallion and data mesh architectures. The goal: Move from CI/CD for individual items to a consistent, predictable, automated lifecycle for interconnected Fabric analytics solutions. Get started with CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse Connect your Warehouse to Git: Set up Git integration to version your Warehouse as a SQL database project and develop changes in isolation. Promote changes across environments: Use deployment pipelines to move Warehouse changes from development to test and production. Automate data actions around your releases: Configure pre and post-deployment scripts so data preparation and seeding travel with your database definition. Integrate with your existing CI/CD systems: Use the Warehouse REST APIs to create, retrieve, and update Warehouse definitions programmatically. Try these capabilities today and share your feedback in Fabric Ideas | Microsoft Fabric Community . Your input directly shapes what we build next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse.
